title: Think Agile before starting Scrum
intro: Understand why short cycles help, and shift your attention from completing a plan to delivering something valuable.

sections.title: Agile: responding to uncertainty
sections.body:
Software teams rarely know everything on day one. User needs and possible solutions can change. Agile uses short cycles to deliver working software, collect feedback, and adjust what happens next.
Agile still involves planning. The difference is that plans change as the team learns. Attending every meeting is not enough if nothing usable is delivered and no improvements follow.
sections.example: A room-booking team first lets students select a room and reserve a time. Feedback reveals that overlapping bookings are the real problem, so the team prioritizes preventing conflicts before building profile pages.
sections.takeaway: Measure progress through working software and the value it creates for users.

sections.title: How to read the four Agile values
sections.body:
Agile values individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; and responding to change over following a plan.
The items on the right still have value. Teams still document, use tools, and plan. These activities should support delivery rather than become obstacles to it.
sections.example: A team has a beautiful task board but never discusses requirements. Members understand the same feature differently. Another tool will not solve this: the team first needs a shared understanding of the goal and acceptance conditions.
sections.takeaway: Tools support collaboration; they cannot replace shared understanding.

sections.title: All twelve Agile principles in practical terms
sections.body:
1. Satisfy customers through early, ongoing delivery of valuable software.
2. Welcome changed needs, including late changes that benefit the customer.
3. Deliver functioning software frequently, favoring shorter intervals.
4. Keep business people and developers collaborating daily.
5. Support motivated people with suitable conditions and trust.
6. Favor face-to-face conversation for effective communication.
7. Judge progress primarily through functioning software.
8. Maintain a pace that all involved can sustain.
9. Keep improving engineering quality and design.
10. Simplify by avoiding unnecessary work.
11. Let teams organize their work so architecture, requirements, and design emerge from their collective knowledge.
12. Reflect regularly and adjust behavior to become more effective.
These are paraphrases, not the original wording. Use the principles together: frequent delivery that sacrifices quality or depends on continual overwork misses their intent.
sections.example: The team notices that manual testing consumes too much time. It adds automated tests for the main booking flow, making changes in the next cycle safer and more reliable.
sections.takeaway: Agile needs both collaboration and engineering capability.

sections.title: Timeboxing: fix the time, choose the scope
sections.body:
A timebox is an agreed limit. When time runs out, the activity ends instead of expanding indefinitely to finish every item. The team must prioritize and choose a scope that fits its capacity.
The classroom DSDM framing fixes time, cost, and agreed quality, then uses feature priorities to manage risk. Quietly reducing quality is not an acceptable response to running out of time. This DSDM framing does not require every Scrum project to adopt an identical fixed-budget model.
sections.example: With three people and two weeks, finish the core booking flow to the agreed quality first. Add theme customization only if time remains. Defer the theme instead of removing conflict checks.
sections.takeaway: Negotiate scope openly rather than silently lowering quality.

sections.title: The three pillars of empiricism
sections.body:
Scrum builds knowledge from experience. Transparency means making information visible and understood consistently. Inspection means examining what is happening against a goal. Adaptation means adjusting when something deviates from expectations.
The pillars work together. Inaccurate information produces misleading inspection; inspecting without adapting wastes the learning opportunity.
sections.example: A board says a feature is finished even though it has not been tested. Agreeing on the meaning of Done makes the information trustworthy, so the team can assess real progress.
sections.takeaway: Transparency → inspection → adaptation is a connected learning cycle.

sections.title: Iterative versus incremental development
sections.body:
Iterative development revisits and improves work using what the team has learned. Incremental development adds usable capabilities in pieces. The two approaches complement each other. They do not mean assigning an entire Sprint to analysis and the next one to design.
Small end-to-end slices expose useful feedback sooner than completing every technical layer separately.
sections.example: Incremental: first deliver room reservations, then add cancellations. Iterative: test the booking screen with users and improve its wording and interaction.
sections.takeaway: Iterate to improve what exists; increment to add usable capability

references.label: Scrum Guide 2020 — Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland

title: See how Scrum works as a whole
intro: Connect the people, work, and events to understand how each part supports valuable delivery.

sections.title: Scrum is a framework
sections.body:
Scrum provides a lightweight structure for tackling complex problems. It does not prescribe every coding step. Teams still choose techniques and practices that fit their situation.
Its central cycle is the Sprint. Each Sprint has a goal and creates a usable Increment, giving the team evidence for learning and future decisions.
The 2020 Guide limits a Sprint to one month; the course describes 1–4 weeks. Keep a consistent cadence and start the next Sprint immediately. Do not insert a separate testing period between Sprints to finish unfinished work.
sections.example: Scrum does not choose React or a database design for you. The team chooses its technology, while making sure the integrated result meets its agreed quality standard.
sections.takeaway: Understand the purpose of the framework before choosing tools.

sections.title: Three accountabilities in the Scrum Team
sections.body:
The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective Product Backlog management. Developers create a usable Increment each Sprint. The Scrum Master helps people understand Scrum and use it effectively.
These accountabilities work together. The Product Owner does not dictate coding methods, and the Scrum Master is not a boss assigning tasks to individuals. Developers manage their plan together.
Developers includes people who help create the Increment, not just programmers. The whole Scrum Team shares accountability for a valuable, usable Increment each Sprint. Delegating backlog-management tasks does not transfer the Product Owner’s accountability.
sections.example: The Product Owner explains why preventing double bookings matters. Developers explore technical options. The Scrum Master helps the team collaborate and address impediments.
sections.takeaway: Keep accountabilities clear while working as one team.

sections.title: Artifacts make work visible
sections.body:
The Product Backlog is an ordered list of work to improve the product, with a Product Goal as its longer-term objective. The Sprint Backlog contains the Sprint Goal, selected items, and the delivery plan. An Increment is a usable result that meets the Definition of Done.
Do not confuse intended work with completed work. Code that has been written but has not met the agreed quality standard is not a Done Increment.
The artifact–commitment pairs are Product Backlog–Product Goal, Sprint Backlog–Sprint Goal, and Increment–Definition of Done. A Sprint can create several Increments. Release can happen before the Review; the Review is not a release gate.
sections.example: “Let students book rooms independently” could be the Product Goal. “Let students see available times and confirm a reservation” could be the first Sprint Goal.
sections.takeaway: The Product Goal, Sprint Goal, and Definition of Done make inspection meaningful.

sections.title: How events connect within a Sprint
sections.body:
Sprint Planning establishes the goal and plan. During the Sprint, Developers build the product and use the Daily Scrum to inspect progress. Near the end, the Sprint Review examines the outcome and product direction with stakeholders; the Sprint Retrospective improves how the team works.
The Sprint contains these events. Development happens throughout the cycle, rather than waiting until every meeting is over.
sections.example: The team plans on Monday, develops and adjusts daily, then invites stakeholders to try the booking system. It also discusses how to reduce delays in code review next Sprint.
sections.takeaway: Each event inspects something different and supports a different kind of adaptation.

sections.title: Review versus Retrospective
sections.body:
The Sprint Review examines product outcomes, progress toward goals, and what to do next in collaboration with stakeholders. It is a working session, rather than simply a presentation for a grade.
The Sprint Retrospective examines quality and effectiveness: people, interactions, practices, tools, and the Definition of Done. The team identifies improvements it can act on.
sections.example: Review: users need building names in the room list → adjust the backlog. Retrospective: integration was left until the final day → agree to integrate work daily.
sections.takeaway: Review adapts product direction; Retrospective improves the way the team works.

sections.title: Pre-game / Game / Post-game: historical course context
sections.body:
Class 2 presents an older description: Pre-game covers initial team, backlog, risk, and architecture planning; Game develops through Sprints; Post-game prepares a release, including documentation and training.
These phases explain historical course material. They are not three Scrum events in the 2020 Guide, and they do not justify postponing all integration and testing until the end: each Sprint’s Increment must meet DoD.
sections.example: Explore the architecture early, but integrate and test the booking UI and API in the Sprint that creates the feature rather than waiting for a final closure phase.
sections.takeaway: Keep the historical course model distinct from the 2020 framework

sections.title: Multilevel planning and just-in-time detail
sections.body:
The course shows Strategy → Portfolio → Product → Release → Sprint → Daily. Distant planning sets direction and constraints; near-term planning adds actionable detail.
Up-front planning still matters, but specifying every task months ahead can waste effort when assumptions change. Balance an overall plan with just-in-time detail. Strategy and Portfolio in the diagram are planning contexts, not additional Scrum artifacts.
sections.example: The product aims to reduce booking effort; the first release supports basic reservations; this Sprint enables confirmation; today’s plan resolves concurrent-booking problems.
sections.takeaway: Plan direction early and add detail close to when it is needed

sections.title: Scrum event timeboxes
sections.body:
Sprint: at most one month in the 2020 Guide; the course uses 1–4 weeks.
Planning: up to eight hours for a month-long Sprint.
Daily Scrum: fifteen minutes each working day.
Review: up to four hours for a month-long Sprint.
Retrospective: up to three hours for a month-long Sprint.
Shorter Sprints usually need shorter Planning, Review, and Retrospective events, but exact proportional scaling is not a rule. The Daily Scrum stays fifteen minutes. Limits are not durations that must be filled.
The Class 2 transcript mentions conflicting Retrospective figures. This lesson uses three hours, matching slide 39 and the 2020 Guide.
sections.example: A two-week Sprint does not require filling four hours of Planning if the team already has a shared goal, selected work, and a practical plan.
sections.takeaway: Understand the purpose as well as the maximum duration

references.label: Scrum Guide 2020 — Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland

title: Turn needs into a Product Backlog
intro: Move from broad ideas to pieces of work that the team can understand, estimate, and order by value.

sections.title: The Product Backlog evolves
sections.body:
The Product Backlog is a source of work for improving the product. It evolves as the team learns. Each Product Backlog Item, or PBI, may represent a feature, a fix, or a necessary improvement.
Items near the top should be clear and small enough for near-term decisions. Distant work can remain broad. The Product Owner is accountable for backlog management and collaborates with Developers and stakeholders.
sections.example: “Room management system” is too broad to develop as one item. As it approaches implementation, the team splits it into viewing availability, making reservations, and cancelling reservations.
sections.takeaway: Add detail when it becomes useful for a decision.

sections.title: User stories start with people and value
sections.body:
A useful thinking pattern is: “As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].” The benefit explains why the capability matters, instead of merely naming a screen or database table.
A story starts a conversation; it does not replace all requirements. Discuss scenarios, constraints, and acceptance conditions together. Not every PBI has to be a user story.
sections.example: As a student, I want to see available room times so that I can choose a booking without repeatedly submitting requests that fail.
sections.takeaway: Explain who benefits from a feature and how.

sections.title: Order work by value and necessity
sections.body:
MoSCoW distinguishes Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won’t have this time. Categories help communicate necessity, but the Product Owner must also order items within each category.
If everything is a Must have, the team has no flexibility when problems arise. Identify the smallest useful set that can be delivered, while considering risks and dependencies.
A Must have is essential for this delivery to be viable, with no acceptable workaround. A Should have matters but can have a temporary workaround. Leaving out a Could have has less impact. Won’t have this time means explicitly excluded from this timeframe, not excluded forever. Revisit priorities for later releases.
sections.example: Must: make bookings without time conflicts. Should: cancel bookings. Could: customize theme colors. When time is short, defer the theme; a system that creates overlapping reservations still misses the goal.
sections.takeaway: Prioritization decides both what to do and what to do first.

sections.title: Refinement prepares work for selection
sections.body:
Product Backlog refinement continuously breaks work down, builds understanding, and adds useful detail, such as description, order, and size. It does not have to wait until Sprint Planning.
The Product Owner explains needs and value; Developers contribute technical understanding and sizing. If the team uses a Definition of Ready, treat it as a local agreement about readiness, rather than a mandatory Scrum artifact.
Refinement also includes adding or removing items, revising estimates, and reordering work as knowledge changes. It is an ongoing activity, not a mandatory sixth Scrum event.
sections.example: “Make a booking” leaves questions unanswered: how far ahead can students book, who may cancel, and how are simultaneous requests handled? The team discusses these before selecting the item.
sections.takeaway: Ready means enough understanding to begin, not complete certainty.

sections.title: Estimate to support planning
sections.body:
Sizing helps compare complexity, effort, and uncertainty. It is not a guarantee of an exact completion time. Developers doing the work are responsible for sizing it; the Product Owner can clarify value and trade-offs.
Large or unclear items may need splitting or investigation. Past delivery data can inform forecasts, but current capacity and context still matter. Avoid using estimates to rank different teams.
Story points and Planning Poker are optional techniques, not Scrum requirements. Avoid treating a point as a fixed number of hours or using velocity to score individual performance.
sections.example: Showing a list of rooms is familiar work. Preventing concurrent requests from double-booking a room introduces more uncertainty, even if the screen has only one button.
sections.takeaway: Screen size is not work size, and an estimate is not a guaranteed deadline.

sections.title: DEEP: useful Product Backlog characteristics
sections.body:
Detailed appropriately: near-term items are smaller and clearer than distant ones.
Emergent: the backlog changes as understanding develops.
Estimated: estimates support decisions and can be revised.
Prioritized: order considers value, size, risk, and fast learning.
Appropriate detail concerns how much detail is useful at a given horizon; emergence concerns changes in content and understanding. DEEP is a course heuristic, not an additional Scrum artifact or event.
sections.example: Confirmation work for the next Sprint is detailed; room recommendations planned much later remain broad. New evidence about booking conflicts can change the order or remove old ideas.
sections.takeaway: Keep detail appropriate, content adaptable, estimates useful, and order clear

sections.title: Split PBIs into useful slices, not just technical layers
sections.body:
A smaller PBI should still enable usable behavior and demonstrable value. UI, API, and database tasks describe implementation work within an item; separate layers do not automatically become valuable user stories.
The course suggests splitting by operations, roles, data or parameters, workflow, happy/unhappy paths, business rules, and basic versus optimized behavior. Check dependencies and required quality; splitting does not permit bypassing essential safety conditions.
sections.example: Split “manage bookings” into “students cancel their own reservations” and “staff block room maintenance periods.” Each may contain UI, API, and test tasks. Creating a database table alone does not let a student cancel a booking.
sections.takeaway: Smaller PBIs explain value; tasks explain how to build it

sections.title: Fixed-date releases and Minimum Releasable Features
sections.body:
A fixed release date needs early delivery of important work, genuinely Done features, and a small Must-have set. Minimum Releasable Features (MRFs) are the essential capabilities that make a release viable at its expected value and quality.
Slide 35 suggests roughly 60–70% of allocated release time for MRFs as a heuristic, leaving room for delays and new necessities. This is not a Scrum rule or a guarantee.
With a forecast of 108–132 points, placing Must-have work beyond the conservative boundary makes the release depend on an optimistic outcome. Team-specific point scales do not support direct cross-team comparisons.
sections.example: A hypothetical 70-point MRF set leaves more uncertainty room against a 108-point lower forecast than a 125-point set that depends on an outcome near the upper forecast.
sections.takeaway: A fixed date needs negotiable scope and essential features that truly reach Done

references.label: Scrum Guide 2020 — Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland

title: Make the Sprint deliver
intro: Set a goal, select realistic work, and turn progress into something usable within the cycle.

sections.title: Sprint Planning answers Why / What / How
sections.body:
Why: what value should this Sprint create, and what is the Sprint Goal? What: which PBIs can fit the team’s capacity? How: how will Developers create the Increment, including any useful task breakdown?
The goal guides decisions during the Sprint. If the original plan no longer works, Developers discuss scope with the Product Owner while protecting the goal, rather than accepting every new request immediately.
Distinguish commitment to the Sprint Goal from the forecast of selected work. Selection is not a guarantee that every item will finish. Developers select work in discussion with the Product Owner and own the implementation plan; the Scrum Master does not impose a workload. If the goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.
sections.example: Goal: students can reserve rooms without conflicts. The team selects availability and confirmation items, then breaks them into UI, API, and concurrency-testing tasks.
sections.takeaway: The Sprint Goal explains why these items belong together.

sections.title: Acceptance Criteria and the Definition of Done
sections.body:
Acceptance Criteria describe item-specific behavior. The Definition of Done describes the shared quality standard that the Increment must meet.
Passing a few functional conditions does not make an item Done if integration, testing, or another agreed standard is missing. Work that fails the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
An item that fails DoD must not be released or presented at the Review as completed Increment work. Organizational DoD standards are a minimum; multiple Scrum Teams working on one product need a shared DoD.
sections.example: Acceptance Criterion: if a time slot is already booked, another booking must not be created. DoD: code reviewed, agreed tests passed, and the feature integrated with the existing system.
sections.takeaway: Criteria describe specific behavior; Done establishes shared quality.

sections.title: Flow management: finish before starting more
sections.body:
When everyone starts more work at once, many items remain in progress while little becomes usable. Look at the flow of each PBI from start to Done, reducing waiting and handoffs.
Swarming means helping complete an item that has already started, by taking remaining tasks or removing obstacles. It does not require everyone to edit the same line. Pair programming can also support collaboration and shared understanding.
sections.example: After finishing the UI, a developer helps with tests and API integration instead of immediately opening another PBI. This helps the first booking feature reach Done sooner.
sections.takeaway: Value comes from finished work, not the amount of work started.

sections.title: Use the Daily Scrum to adapt the daily plan
sections.body:
The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog into an actionable plan. The team chooses a useful format.
It is not a status report to a manager. Detailed problem-solving can continue afterward with the relevant people. Impediments should be raised when discovered, rather than saved for tomorrow’s meeting.
Hold it each working day at a consistent time and place. The course offers five prompts: yesterday’s work, today’s plan, impediments, forgotten work, and learning to share. These prompts are a facilitation option, not a required script in the 2020 Guide.
sections.example: “The booking API has a transaction issue that threatens the goal. Two of us will investigate today while another prepares tests” is more useful than listing yesterday’s coding hours.
sections.takeaway: Leave the Daily Scrum knowing how to move forward together.

sections.title: Read the board to spot problems
sections.body:
A To do / In progress / Done board makes status visible, but only if people update it and share the same definitions. Track PBIs as well as tasks: many completed tasks do not necessarily mean usable delivery.
When work stalls, ask what it is waiting for, who can help, and how it affects the Sprint Goal. Adapt the plan instead of waiting until the Review to reveal that the work is not ready.
sections.example: Four of five tasks are complete, but the final task tests booking conflicts. Until that task and the agreed quality checks pass, the PBI should not move to Done.
sections.takeaway: Status should reflect reality well enough to support decisions.

sections.title: Capacity and buffer: calendar hours are not all available
sections.body:
Capacity is realistic availability. Account for holidays, leave, training, other work, and relevant events instead of assuming eight uninterrupted development hours per person per day.
A buffer allows for unplanned work and estimation error. Calibrate it using experience across Sprints rather than imposing one universal percentage. Avoid silently adding the same contingency to every task and again to the total.
Effort-hours and story points describe different things. Use capacity and past delivery evidence to forecast without a fixed conversion formula.
sections.example: Hypothetical example: three people with ten working days each have 30 person-days. Five person-days of leave and training leave 25 before routine work, events, and uncertainty. That is not 25 fully available development days.
sections.takeaway: Start with actual availability and make uncertainty visible

sections.title: Spikes: reduce uncertainty before selecting risky work
sections.body:
A spike investigates a question through a prototype, proof of concept, experiment, or study. Technical spikes explore implementation; functional spikes explore desired behavior and edge cases.
Define the question, expected learning, and a time limit. The result should support a decision, splitting, or a revised estimate. A prototype does not automatically qualify as a production Increment. A spike is not a mandatory Scrum event.
Class 4 suggests investigating future-Sprint work ahead of time in the student project; not every PBI must first have a spike.
sections.example: A technical spike compares transaction approaches for simultaneous bookings. A functional spike investigates how a waiting list receives cancelled slots. The outcome is actionable findings, not just time spent reading.
sections.takeaway: Use a spike to answer a specific question and reduce uncertainty

references.label: Scrum Guide 2020 — Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland

title: Build a team that trusts and improves
intro: Scrum values appear in everyday behavior, from helping teammates to speaking openly about problems.

sections.title: The five Scrum values in practice
sections.body:
Commitment: support goals and the team. Focus: concentrate on important Sprint work. Openness: share work and challenges. Respect: value other people’s capabilities and perspectives. Courage: do the right thing and address difficult problems.
These values build trust and make transparency, inspection, and adaptation possible. They should shape behavior, rather than remain words on a wall.
sections.example: A developer realizes an estimate was too optimistic and tells the team immediately. Others listen without blame, help adapt the plan, and decide what to discuss with the Product Owner.
sections.takeaway: Speaking openly about problems takes courage, respect, and trust.

sections.title: Working group versus working team
sections.body:
A working group often divides tasks and combines the results. A working team also shares a goal, complementary skills, and mutual accountability for the overall outcome, while retaining individual responsibility.
“My part is finished” is not the end if the team’s Increment still cannot be used. Helping with a bottleneck is part of teamwork.
sections.example: The frontend is ready, but the API is blocked. A team focused on its shared goal helps test, investigate, and reduce the remaining work so users can actually book rooms.
sections.takeaway: Take responsibility for your own contribution and the team’s outcome.

sections.title: Self-managing and cross-functional
sections.body:
Self-managing means the team decides internally who does what, when, and how within its shared goals. Cross-functional means the team collectively has the skills needed to create value without handing every step to an outside specialist.
Everyone does not need identical expertise. People should learn, collaborate, and reduce bottlenecks caused by depending on one person. Pairing and knowledge-sharing help build that capability.
sections.example: Only one person knows how to deploy. The team pairs on deployments and writes a short guide so others can step in when that person is unavailable.
sections.takeaway: Team autonomy depends on shared capabilities and shared decisions.

sections.title: Technical debt and refactoring
sections.body:
Technical debt is the future burden created by technical choices that make changes harder or more expensive. A team may deliberately accept debt for a short-term benefit, but should make the cost visible and plan how to manage it.
Refactoring improves internal structure without changing observable behavior, for example by removing duplication, extracting functions, or improving names. Technical debt does not justify calling work Done when it fails the Definition of Done.
sections.example: Booking-conflict checks are duplicated in three places. Changing a rule requires editing all three. The team extracts a shared function and uses tests to confirm that behavior remains unchanged.
sections.takeaway: Internal quality protects the ability to change the product over time.

sections.title: The Scrum Master helps the team think and improve
sections.body:
The Scrum Master coaches self-management and cross-functionality, helps Scrum events become useful, and helps address impediments to progress.
Coaching uses questions to help the team explore problems and options rather than dictating every answer. Support for the Product Owner and organization should respect their accountabilities, without taking over product ordering or technical decisions.
sections.example: Instead of ordering overtime, the Scrum Master asks where work is waiting and whether limiting work in progress or swarming could help. The team then experiments with its chosen approach.
sections.takeaway: Help the team become able to decide and improve for itself.

sections.title: The Trust Equation: expertise alone is not enough
sections.body:
The Trusted Advisor model shown in class is Trustworthiness = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-orientation.
Credibility concerns believable words and expertise. Reliability concerns following through. Intimacy concerns feeling safe sharing vulnerability. Self-orientation concerns focusing on oneself rather than others.
Use it to discuss behavior, not as an exact scientific scoring formula or a Scrum artifact. Technical expertise does not automatically compensate for broken promises or making teammates afraid to disclose mistakes.
sections.example: An expert who hides work and blames others may be less trusted than someone who admits limits, keeps agreements, and makes it safe to discuss mistakes.
sections.takeaway: Trust depends on capability, follow-through, and care for others

sections.title: Responsibility, accountability, efficiency, and effectiveness
sections.body:
Responsibility concerns duties and tasks; accountability concerns ownership of outcomes. Dividing tasks does not remove shared responsibility for the result.
Accountability is not universally limited to one person: the Product Owner is individually accountable for product value and backlog management, while the Scrum Team has shared accountability for the Increment. A working team combines individual and mutual accountability.
Efficiency concerns resource use; effectiveness concerns achieving the intended result. A team can implement an unwanted feature quickly and still fail its goal.
sections.example: One person writes the API, but the team must make the integrated booking flow work. Fast API delivery does not meet the goal if the system still creates duplicate bookings.
sections.takeaway: Separate assigned duties from outcomes, and speed from achieving the goal

sections.title: T-shaped skills and a sustainable team
sections.body:
T-shaped skills combine depth in a specialty with enough breadth to collaborate beyond it. This helps reduce handoffs and enables swarming without requiring everyone to be equally expert in every area.
The course also emphasizes rich, transparent communication, mutual support, a sustainable pace, and long-lived teams that develop shared understanding.
Slide 19 cites the 2020 Guide’s typical Scrum Team size of ten or fewer. Slide 30 gives an older five-to-nine development-team heuristic. These describe different contexts; neither means a three-person student team cannot collaborate effectively.
sections.example: A frontend specialist learns enough API and test work to help resolve integration issues, while a backend specialist explains data constraints clearly. Work no longer waits on one expert at every step.
sections.takeaway: Combine specialist depth with the breadth needed to help teammates
